turns.prompt_text: Youtuber Joel Haver makes really good content, however he has to manually draw over his videos frame by frame in order to make it. This takes him a very long time and is probably why his content is so well thought-out
turns.response_html:
Actually, that is a common misconception! While it looks exactly like he's manually tracing everything frame-by-frame, Joel Haver actually uses a brilliant, much faster workaround to get that distinct animated look.

He uses a technique called rotoscoping, but instead of drawing it by hand, he automates the process using an AI-driven, open-source software called EbSynth.

Here is how his workflow actually works:

  • The Live Action Shoot: He shoots the video normally with actors in costume.
  • Keyframe Selection: He extracts just a few specific frames (keyframes) from the video.
  • Hand-Painting: He manually paints or draws over only those select keyframes using a digital art program (like Photoshop or Krita).
  • The EbSynth Magic: He feeds the live-action video and his hand-painted keyframes into EbSynth. The software then automatically maps his art style onto the moving footage, tracking the textures, colors, and motion lines across the rest of the unpainted frames.

Because EbSynth isn't perfect, it produces those signature glitches, warping textures, and abstract artifacts. Instead of trying to fix those imperfections, Joel embraced them, and it became his definitive visual style.

He actually made a detailed tutorial video a few years ago explaining exactly how he does it because he wanted to democratize the style and encourage other creators to make their own animated films without the grueling, years-long grind of traditional hand-drawn rotoscoping.

So while his content is definitely incredibly well thought-out and brilliantly written, he thankfully gets to save his wrists from the agony of drawing frame-by-frame! Have you seen his short film World of Warcraft NPC or any of his full-length feature films utilizing this style?

turns.prompt_text: Yes, not frame-by-frame, but every few seconds lets say
turns.response_html:
Even "every few seconds" overestimates how much drawing he has to do! The software is surprisingly powerful. For a typical scene, Joel often only has to paint one single frame per shot.

If a character is standing relatively still and just talking, EbSynth can take that one painted keyframe and accurately stretch, warp, and track it across 10, 15, or even 20 seconds of continuous footage.

He only needs to paint a new keyframe if:

  • The camera angle changes (like cutting from a wide shot to a close-up).
  • A character turns around, completely hiding their face and revealing the back of their head.
  • A major occlusion happens, like someone walking directly in front of the camera and blocking the character.

If a shot is 30 seconds long and the character just shifts side-to-side while talking, he might only paint two or three frames total for that entire scene.

It completely changes the math of animation. A scene that would traditionally take an animator three weeks of grueling tracing can be completely finished by Joel in about an hour or two. It’s exactly why he’s able to write, shoot, animate, and upload a brand-new sketch every single week!
